# How Database Transactions Recover After a Power Failure

When a database server loses power, the situation is fundamentally different from a clean shutdown. The database cannot rely on in-memory state being flushed to disk, because the operating system may have buffered writes, and the process is killed abruptly. Recovery after a power failure is therefore not about "undoing" a transaction that was in progress in a controlled way—it is about reconstructing a consistent state from whatever durable artifacts exist on disk. This article explains the mechanisms databases use, with worked examples, and discusses the limitations of these approaches.

# How a Compiler Detects and Optimizes Repeated Expressions

Repeated expressions are one of the most common sources of wasted computation in programs. A compiler that can recognize when the same value has already been computed can eliminate redundant work, sometimes turning an O(n²) loop into an O(n) one. This article explains the core mechanisms—local value numbering, global value numbering, and loop-invariant code motion—with worked examples, and then discusses the limitations that keep these optimizations from being universally applicable.

# How TCP Congestion Control Adapts to Changing Bandwidth

TCP congestion control is the set of algorithms a TCP sender uses to infer the available capacity of the network path and to adjust its sending rate accordingly. Because the network is a shared, dynamic resource—links change capacity due to radio conditions, cross-traffic, and routing changes—the core challenge is that a sender has no direct knowledge of the bottleneck's bandwidth. It must infer it from feedback. This document explains the mechanisms, walks through concrete numerical examples, and discusses where the approach breaks down.
